cards.back: Metrics tell you that something is wrong, traces tell you where, and logs tell you why. Real systems collect all three and link them by a shared request ID.
Monitoring answers questions you thought of in advance. Observability is the wider goal of answering questions you did not think of from the data you already collect.
RED (rate, errors, duration) is for anything that serves requests. USE (utilisation, saturation, errors) is for resources like CPU, disks and connection pools.
An average hides the slow tail: 99 requests at 50 ms and one at 5 s average about 100 ms. Track p50, p95 and p99, and store latency as histograms so you can combine servers correctly.
Every distinct set of labels is its own time series, so cost grows with label combinations, not traffic. Keep unbounded values like user IDs and full URLs in logs and traces, not metric labels.
An SLI is good events over all events, measured from the user's side. An SLO is the target over a window, usually 28 or 30 days, and the error budget is 1 − SLO.
Observed error rate divided by (1 − SLO). A burn rate of 1 spends the budget exactly by the end of the window; 10 spends a 30-day budget in 3 days.

cards.front: Why a Kafka buffer in the log pipeline?
cards.back: When an incident makes every service log ten times more, the buffer grows instead of the log store falling over. Agents tail stdout, ship to Kafka, and indexers load the searchable store.
Every call must carry the trace ID and parent span ID, via the W3C traceparent header over HTTP and gRPC or message headers through a queue. One hop that drops it splits the trace.
Head sampling decides at the first service, cheaply, but keeps only a share of errors too. Tail sampling buffers a trace's spans then decides, so it can keep every error and slow trace.
Page for what users feel: errors and slowness on the SLI. High CPU with happy users is fine, and an outage from a bad config may never move CPU.
An alert that is always firing, so the pager provider pages you if it stops hearing it. It catches the case where monitoring shares the outage.

quiz.q: A page makes 20 backend calls. About how often does a load hit at least one call's p99?
How much downtime does a 99.9% SLO allow in 30 days?
Why can't you average 50 servers' p99 latencies to get the fleet p99?
choices: Percentiles don't average; merge histograms then take the p99
Each server uses a different clock
Averages are only valid for counters
quiz.why: Histograms (counts per bucket) add up; pre-computed percentiles do not.

quiz.q: Adding a user_id label with a million users to a request metric will most likely do what?
choices: Explode cardinality and take down the metrics database
quiz.why: Each label combination is its own series, so it becomes billions of series.

quiz.q: Which page-level alert does the Google SRE workbook pattern use for fast burns?
choices: Burn rate 14.4 over 1 hour and 5 minutes
quiz.why: It fires after spending 2% of the budget and stops soon after the fix.

quiz.q: A service crashes and its error rate drops to zero. What catches this?
choices: Alerts on missing data and synthetic probes
quiz.why: Silence looks like health unless you alert on absent data.

quiz.q: You need a trace for every rare error. Which sampling approach fits?
choices: No sampling of errors, only successes
quiz.why: Head sampling decides before knowing the result, so it may drop the rare error.

quiz.q: 50,000 req/s × 10 log lines × 500 bytes is about how much raw log data a day?
